Transport Layer Security Configuration
WHAT: Misconfigured TLS (weak protocols/ciphers, compression, bad DH groups, mixed HTTP/HTTPS, weak certs/keys, missing HSTS/secure cookies/cache controls) exposes traffic to eavesdropping, tampering, and impersonation.
WHY: Attackers can decrypt or modify data in transit, steal session cookies, obtain rogue certificates, or downgrade connections, leading to account takeover and data disclosure.
HOW: Enable only TLS 1.3 (optionally 1.2) and strong cipher suites (no NULL/anonymous/EXPORT), disable TLS compression, use RFC7919 DH groups, keep crypto libraries patched, use ≥2048-bit keys and SHA-256 certs with correct SANs, avoid overbroad wildcard certs, enforce HTTPS everywhere (HSTS, no HTTP for APIs, no mixed content), set Secure on cookies, disable caching for sensitive responses, and consider mTLS/pinning for high-value internal APIs.
EXAMPLE: Before (server): supports TLS 1.0/1.1, EXPORT ciphers, compression on, HTTP endpoint serving app, cookies without Secure, no HSTS. After (server): only TLS 1.3/1.2 with GCM suites, `ssl_compression off`, RFC7919 DH groups, HTTP 301 to HTTPS + HSTS, API only on HTTPS, all cookies `Set-Cookie: name=value; Secure; HttpOnly`, and `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate` on sensitive responses.
Abuse-case–driven security requirements
WHAT: Failing to explicitly identify and track abuse cases for each feature leads to missing or incomplete security requirements and unprotected business logic paths.
WHY: Unidentified abuse cases allow attackers to misuse functionality (e.g., price changes, malicious uploads) and bypass controls, causing data loss, fraud, or service compromise.
HOW: For every feature/user story, run a structured workshop (business, risk, technical, AppSec, pentest) to enumerate technical and business abuse cases, rate their risk, define concrete countermeasures and locations (network/infrastructure/code), assign unique IDs, and add them as explicit security requirements or acceptance criteria; track implementation via code annotations/comments and validate with targeted tests and reviews.
EXAMPLE: Before: Implement `DocumentUploadFeature` with no documented abuse cases or countermeasures. After: Define `ABUSE_CASE_001` “Upload Office file with malicious macro,” add requirement “DEFENSE_001: validate uploaded files via a safe parser per file-upload guidelines,” annotate the upload handler with `@AbuseCase(ids={"ABUSE_CASE_001"})`, and add tests that attempt to upload malicious documents.
Vulnerability disclosure process for software projects
WHAT: Inadequate or ad‑hoc handling of reported vulnerabilities (e.g., no secure contact channel, unclear scope, or poor communication) leads to unfixed security bugs and uncoordinated public disclosure.
WHY: Unmanaged disclosure increases window of exposure, enables easier exploitation (especially when details or PoC are public before a patch), and damages trust with users and researchers.
HOW: Publish clear disclosure and/or bug bounty policies (scope, safe harbor, timelines, rewards), provide secure reporting channels (e.g., security@, security.txt, PGP), triage reports promptly, communicate status and timelines, and issue security advisories with affected/fixed versions and mitigations.
EXAMPLE: Not language-specific; define and document a project-wide “Security Policy” and “Security Advisories” process, and ensure developers know how to receive, triage, fix, and publish information about vulnerabilities.
Cookie theft detection and mitigation for session cookies
WHAT: Session cookies can be stolen and reused from a different environment (IP, device, headers), allowing full session hijacking until expiry if the server only checks cookie validity.
WHY: An attacker with a valid stolen session cookie can impersonate the user, access confidential data, and perform sensitive actions despite strong primary authentication.
HOW: On session creation, persist server-side metadata (IP, User-Agent, Accept-Language, Date, and other stable headers); on each request, compare current values to stored ones, detect significant changes, and on suspicion require additional verification (CAPTCHA and/or re-authentication) and issue a new session cookie; apply stricter checks on high-risk endpoints.
EXAMPLE:
Before: `app.post("/users/delete", handler)` (only checks cookie value).
After: `app.post("/users/delete", cookieTheftDetectionMiddleware, handler)` where the middleware compares `req.clientIP`, `req.headers['user-agent']`, etc. to session-stored values and triggers re-auth/CAPTCHA on large deviations.
XML parsing and schema validation security
WHAT: XML parsers and schemas can be abused via malformed/invalid documents, entity expansion (XXE/Billion Laughs), jumbo payloads, and schema poisoning to cause DoS, data corruption, SSRF, and local file disclosure.
WHY: Unbounded parsing, external entities, weak schemas, and tamperable DTD/XSD let attackers exhaust CPU/memory, bypass business rules, read local files, scan internal networks, or alter validation rules.
HOW: Use standards-compliant parsers with recovery disabled; disable DTDs and all external entities/parameter entities; enforce strict local XSD schemas (no remote/HTTP refs, integrity-checked, least-privilege filesystem perms); bound depth/width, occurrences, payload size, and entity expansion; use precise data types (e.g., positiveInteger, decimal, base64Binary) plus length/range/pattern/enumeration/assertion constraints; require TLS and robust DNS validation for any unavoidable remote schema access.
EXAMPLE: In Java, before: `DocumentBuilderFactory f = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();` (defaults allow DTD/XXE). After: `f.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true); f.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities", false); f.setFeature("http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities", false); f.setXIncludeAware(false); f.setExpandEntityReferences(false);` and validate against a strict local XSD.
Node.js secure coding guidelines
WHAT: Node.js applications are exposed to common web vulnerabilities (injection, XSS, CSRF, DoS, brute force, info leakage, etc.) if code, configuration, and dependencies are not written and maintained with security in mind.
WHY: Exploiting these weaknesses can lead to remote code execution, data theft, account takeover, denial of service, and unauthorized access to files or functionality.
HOW: Validate and sanitize all inputs; escape outputs; set request size limits; avoid blocking the event loop and race conditions; use promises/async‑await correctly; enforce rate limiting, CAPTCHA, and account lockout; use CSRF protection; remove unused/auto‑generated routes; prevent HTTP parameter pollution; minimize returned fields; configure cookie flags and security headers; keep dependencies updated; avoid dangerous APIs (eval, child_process.exec, unsafe fs/vm use, evil regexes); enable strict mode, ACLs, and Node.js permissions; handle errors and EventEmitter failures safely; log securely; and monitor event loop load.
EXAMPLE: For example, in Express, combine middleware such as helmet(), nocache(), express.json({limit: '1kb'}), hpp(), rate limiting on /login, CSRF protection, strict cookie settings, and careful route definitions, while avoiding eval/exec and validating all user-controlled data before using it in queries, file paths, or commands.
Error Handling and Information Leakage
WHAT: Unhandled exceptions and verbose error responses that include stack traces, SQL errors, file paths, or technology/version details are sent to clients instead of a generic error message.
WHY: Detailed error information enables reconnaissance, helps identify injection points, and exposes implementation details that attackers can exploit.
HOW: Configure a global error handler to catch all unexpected exceptions, log full details server-side, and return only generic, implementation-agnostic error responses (e.g., RFC 7807 problem details) with appropriate 4xx/5xx codes; disable or restrict detailed error pages in non-development environments.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java): `throw e;` → framework returns full stack trace to user. After: use a global `@RestControllerAdvice` with `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` that logs `exception` and returns `ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "An error occurred, please retry");`.
Java Bean Validation for Secure Input Handling
WHAT: Failure to validate user-controlled input on model fields, parameters, and return values can allow malformed, unexpected, or malicious data to enter the application.
WHY: Unvalidated or weakly validated input can lead to injection, data integrity issues, and logic abuse across application layers.
HOW: Apply appropriate Bean Validation constraints (@Pattern, @Digits, @Size, @Min/@Max, @Past/@Future, etc.) on all user-controlled fields and enable cascading validation with @Valid on controllers, parameters, and nested beans; avoid deprecated constraints like @SafeHtml and prefer current, well-maintained validators.
EXAMPLE: Before (no validation): `public class Article { private String articleTitle; }` After (validated): `public class Article { @Pattern(regexp = "[a-zA-Z0-9 ]") private String articleTitle; }`
Secure logging and tamper-resistant log storage
WHAT: Logs from applications and infrastructure must not be modifiable or deletable by a compromised system that generates them; only append-only logging is allowed from those systems.
WHY: If an attacker can alter or erase logs on a compromised host, incident detection, forensics, and compliance evidence are lost or unreliable.
HOW: Forward logs in near real time to a dedicated logging server or cluster on a separate network segment; use protocols and configurations that only allow appending new events (e.g., syslog with append-only permissions), and deny write/delete access to existing log files from application hosts.
EXAMPLE: Application host → sends logs via syslog to central log server; log server filesystem and ACLs are configured so application host accounts can only send new log entries over the network and cannot modify or delete stored logs.
Insecure deserialization of untrusted data
WHAT: Deserializing untrusted or user-controlled data with native or unsafe mechanisms (e.g., PHP unserialize, Python pickle/PyYAML/jsonpickle, Java ObjectInputStream/XMLDecoder/XStream, .NET BinaryFormatter/unsafe JSON.Net settings, unsafe fastjson/Kryo/SnakeYAML/etc.) can instantiate arbitrary classes, trigger gadget chains, or clobber sensitive fields.
WHY: Attackers can achieve remote code execution, denial of service, access control bypass, or data leakage by steering which types are deserialized or by abusing dangerous properties and custom deserialization logic.
HOW: Avoid native object deserialization for untrusted data; prefer pure data formats (JSON/XML) and safe libraries/configs (e.g., JSON in PHP; Python yaml.safe_load; Java hardened ObjectInputStream with strict allowlist and length/object-count checks; .NET DataContractSerializer/XmlSerializer with TypeNameHandling=None and no JavaScriptTypeResolver; enable safemode/registration/safe constructors in fastjson/Kryo/SnakeYAML/etc.; declare sensitive Java fields private transient; for classes that must be Serializable but must not be deserialized, implement a final readObject that always throws; only deserialize signed/authenticated data; never let user input control the target type.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java, unsafe): `ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(untrustedStream); Object obj = ois.readObject();`
After (Java, hardened): `ObjectInputStream ois = new LookAheadObjectInputStream(untrustedStream);` where `resolveClass` only allows specific expected types and throws `InvalidClassException` for all others.
Microservices authorization and identity propagation
WHAT: In microservices, relying only on edge-level authorization, hardcoding authorization rules in service code, reusing external access tokens internally, or sending caller identity as clear/self-signed data structures can lead to bypassed access control, outdated policies, token leakage, and privilege escalation.
WHY: These issues can allow attackers to call internal services directly, use leaked tokens, exploit stale or inconsistent policies, or forge identities/roles, resulting in unauthorized access, data exposure, and broken defense-in-depth.
HOW: Implement defense-in-depth by enforcing coarse-grained authorization at the gateway and fine-grained checks at service and business-code levels using shared libraries/components and a centralized, embedded PDP; externalize policies in a dedicated policy language and manage them via PAP/PDP/PEP/PIP; propagate identity using an internal, extensible data structure signed/encrypted by a trusted issuer at the edge (never expose it externally), and avoid passing external tokens directly to internal services or trusting caller-supplied identity fields.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): internal service accepts and validates the same JWT used by browsers and trusts roles from HTTP headers set by callers. After (more secure): edge service validates the external JWT, builds a signed internal “passport” with user ID and roles, attaches it to internal requests; each microservice verifies the signature using a shared key, enforces authorization via a common library that queries an embedded PDP loaded with centrally managed policies.
LDAP Injection Prevention for LDAP Queries
WHAT: Untrusted input is concatenated into LDAP DNs or search filters without proper escaping or validation, allowing attackers to alter queries (LDAP injection) and gain unauthorized access or modify directory data.
WHY: LDAP injection can expose sensitive directory information, grant permissions to unauthorized users, or allow modification of LDAP content, undermining authentication and authorization.
HOW: Never build LDAP queries by string concatenation with raw user input; instead, (1) escape all untrusted values with the correct LDAP encoding for their context (DN vs search filter) using vetted APIs (e.g., encodeForLDAP/encodeForDN, Encoder.LdapFilterEncode/LdapDistinguishedNameEncode), (2) apply strict allow‑list validation and normalization to all LDAP-related inputs, (3) use frameworks that automatically encode LDAP parameters (e.g., LINQ to LDAP), and (4) run LDAP operations under least-privilege service accounts and require bind authentication.
EXAMPLE: In Java, validate and encode before use:
Before: `String filter = "(&(sn=" + userSN + ")(userPassword=" + userPassword + "))";`
After:  `String filter = "(&(sn=" + encodeForLDAP(userSN) + ")(userPassword=" + encodeForLDAP(userPassword) + "))";`
gRPC Service Security Guidelines
WHAT: In gRPC services, insecure transport, weak authz/authn, missing input validation, unbounded resources, verbose errors, and exposed reflection can lead to eavesdropping, injection, DoS, and information disclosure.
WHY: Attackers can steal data, impersonate services/users, exhaust CPU/memory, pivot via internal APIs, and gain detailed knowledge of your service surface.
HOW: Always use TLS 1.2+ with strong ciphers and mTLS for service-to-service calls; enforce per-method authentication (JWT/API keys with short-lived tokens in metadata) and least-privilege authorization; validate all protobuf fields with allowlists and parameterized queries; set strict message size limits, rate limits, and timeouts; return generic errors while logging details; disable reflection in production and secure service discovery (mTLS/RBAC/mesh); monitor security metrics and add gRPC-specific tests to CI.
EXAMPLE: In Go, wrap servers with security interceptors and TLS:
Before: `s := grpc.NewServer()`
After: `creds, _ := credentials.NewServerTLSFromFile(certFile, keyFile); s := grpc.NewServer(grpc.Creds(creds), grpc.MaxRecvMsgSize(4*1024*1024), grpc.UnaryInterceptor(authInterceptor))`
Software Supply Chain Security in Development and Build Processes
WHAT: Risk of compromised source code, dependencies, build tools, and CI/CD configurations leading to injection of malicious code, use of vulnerable components, or tampered artifacts throughout the software supply chain.
WHY: Successful supply chain attacks can compromise confidentiality, integrity, and availability across many downstream systems, enabling code execution, data theft, and large-scale propagation of malicious updates.
HOW: Enforce least privilege, MFA, and secret hygiene on VCS/CI/CD; require peer review and protected branches; inventory and harden IDEs, plugins, build tools, and build infrastructure; rigorously assess and pin third‑party dependencies; generate and verify provenance and code signatures; use private artifact repositories and ephemeral, isolated build environments; centralize logging/monitoring and automate SAST/SCA and binary scanning.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): CI pulls latest dependency versions with no lockfile, builds on a long‑lived shared runner, pushes unsigned artifacts directly from a developer machine. After (more secure): CI uses a pinned lockfile, runs builds in disposable containers, stores build scripts/configs in VCS with reviews, signs artifacts using a hardened signing service, and publishes only to a controlled private repository with provenance metadata.
Authentication error messages and timing
WHAT: Authentication endpoints (login, password reset, registration) return different messages, HTTP status codes, or response times depending on whether a username/email exists, the password is wrong, or the account state, enabling user enumeration and timing attacks.
WHY: Attackers can discover valid accounts and their status, and use timing differences to distinguish “user exists but wrong password” from “user does not exist,” greatly improving brute-force, credential stuffing, and targeted attacks.
HOW: Always return a single generic error message, identical HTTP status code, and similar processing path and timing for all authentication failures; avoid “quick exit” branches based on user existence, and ensure error pages and APIs do not leak account validity via content, codes, or URLs.
EXAMPLE:
Before:
if (!userExists(u)) return 403, "Login failed; account does not exist";
if (!passwordOk(u,p)) return 403, "Login for user " + u + ": invalid password";
After:
hash = hashPassword(p);
isValid = lookupUserAndPassword(u, hash);
if (!isValid) return 401, "Login failed; Invalid user ID or password";
Laravel security configuration and coding practices
WHAT: Laravel apps can be exposed to mass assignment, SQL injection, XSS, unrestricted file upload, path traversal, open redirect, CSRF, command/object injection, weak cookies/sessions, missing rate limits, and missing security headers when defaults are disabled or user input is used unsafely.
WHY: These issues can lead to privilege escalation (e.g., is_admin changes), data theft or corruption, account hijacking, remote code execution, storage/CPU DoS, credential phishing, and exposure of secrets (e.g., .env).
HOW: Keep APP_DEBUG=false in production, generate APP_KEY, use guarded/fillable and $request->only()/validated(), always parameterize SQL (including whereRaw), never let user input choose column names or validation columns, escape output (avoid {!! !!} on untrusted data), validate upload type/size and strip paths (basename) from filenames, strip paths from download filenames, validate/allowlist redirect targets, keep VerifyCsrfToken + @csrf on stateful routes, never pass untrusted data to exec/eval/unserialize/extract, enable cookie encryption, HttpOnly, SameSite, secure flags and reasonable session lifetimes, apply throttle middleware/RateLimiter, and add X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, HSTS, and CSP headers.
EXAMPLE: // Insecure (mass assignment)
// $request->user()->forceFill($request->all())->save();
// Secure
$data = $request->only(['name','email']); $request->user()->update($data);
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Output Handling and Sanitization
WHAT: Untrusted data is inserted into HTML, attributes, JavaScript, CSS, URLs, or dangerous sinks (e.g., innerHTML, event handlers, eval) without proper context-specific encoding or sanitization, allowing attacker-controlled script execution in the browser.
WHY: Successful XSS enables account takeover, data theft, user impersonation, external content loading, and arbitrary actions in the victim’s session, often bypassing other security controls.
HOW: For all untrusted data, first validate input, then apply context-appropriate output encoding (HTML entity for HTML body, HTML-attribute encoding for attributes, JS encoding for quoted JS values, CSS encoding for CSS properties, URL encoding for URL parts). Avoid placing variables in dangerous contexts (event handlers, javascript: URLs, inline script blocks, style selectors). Prefer framework auto-escaping and safe sinks (textContent, setAttribute with safe attributes, style.property, encodeURIComponent). When users must author HTML, sanitize with a maintained library (e.g., DOMPurify) and do not mutate sanitized content afterward; keep sanitization libraries patched.
EXAMPLE:
Before (unsafe HTML/JS/URL):
`elem.innerHTML = userInput;`
`<a href="?q=` + userInput + `">search</a>`
After (safe sinks + encoding/sanitization):
`elem.textContent = userInput;`
`<a href="?q=` + encodeURIComponent(userInput) + `">search</a>`
`elem.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(userHtmlInput);`
Content Security Policy (CSP) for Web Applications
WHAT: Failure to define and correctly enforce a Content-Security-Policy header (or meta tag when headers are unavailable) allows inline scripts, arbitrary remote scripts, eval-like functions, untrusted form targets, plugin objects, and hostile framing, enabling XSS, clickjacking, and cross-site leaks.
WHY: Missing or weak CSP lets attackers inject and execute malicious code, exfiltrate data via forms or network calls, load compromised third-party resources, and frame your site for phishing or clickjacking.
HOW: Send a CSP header on all responses; prefer a strict, nonce- or hash-based policy with script-src 'strict-dynamic', object-src 'none', base-uri 'none', and tightly scoped default-src/script-src/img-src/style-src/connect-src; disallow 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval'; restrict form-action and frame-ancestors; use Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only plus reporting endpoints to tune policies safely; avoid obsolete X-* CSP headers.
EXAMPLE: Before (weak): Content-Security-Policy: default-src * 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval';
After (strict): Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'nonce-{RANDOM}' 'strict-dynamic'; img-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'; form-action 'self';
Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Protection
WHAT: CSRF occurs when an attacker causes a victim’s authenticated browser or client-side code to send unintended state-changing requests; failures include missing/invalid CSRF tokens, unsafe use of attacker-controlled input to build requests, and misuse of cookies/CORS that allows forged requests.
WHY: Successful CSRF lets attackers perform any action the victim is authorized to do (e.g., money transfers, password changes, purchases, privilege changes), or hijack sessions (including via login CSRF or cookie injection), even when authentication is otherwise correct.
HOW: Use your framework’s built-in CSRF protection where available; otherwise, for all state-changing operations (never using GET unless strictly necessary and then protected) implement one of: (a) synchronizer token pattern with server-generated, secret, unpredictable tokens validated per request/session and never sent in URLs or cookies; (b) signed double-submit cookies with HMAC tokens bound to session-specific data and verified in constant time; or (c) custom non-simple request headers plus strict CORS allowlists for controlled origins. Additionally, enforce SameSite and Secure cookie attributes (prefer __Host- prefix where possible), avoid setting cookies for parent domains, validate Origin/Referer against a strict allowlist, and for client-side code never derive request methods/endpoints directly from attacker-controlled inputs (URL, window.name, referrer, postMessage, etc.) without strict allowlists and format checks. For highly sensitive actions, add user interaction defenses such as re-authentication or one-time tokens, and for login forms use pre-session CSRF tokens that are discarded and replaced on successful authentication.
EXAMPLE: (JavaScript, synchronizer token via custom header)
Before (vulnerable):
```javascript
// State-changing POST without CSRF protection
fetch('/transfer', {
method: 'POST',
credentials: 'include',
body: JSON.stringify({ to: '123', amount: 100 })
});
```
After (protected):
```javascript
// CSRF token injected into DOM by server: <meta name="csrf-token" content="{{token}}">
const token = document.querySelector('meta[name="csrf-token"]').content;
fetch('/transfer', {
method: 'POST',
credentials: 'include',
headers: { 'X-CSRF-Token': token, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
body: JSON.stringify({ to: '123', amount: 100 })
});
```
SAML message and assertion security
WHAT: SAML implementations may expose users to eavesdropping, token theft, forged or modified assertions, XML signature wrapping, replay, and open redirect if messages, signatures, protocol fields, bindings, and inputs are not strictly validated and protected.
WHY: Exploitation can lead to account takeover, impersonation across trusted partners, session hijacking, data disclosure, and abuse of SSO trust relationships between IdPs and SPs.
HOW: Enforce TLS 1.2+ for all SAML endpoints; require signed responses/assertions with keys obtained out-of-band and ignore in-document KeyInfo; encrypt assertions containing sensitive data; strictly follow SAML Core/Profiles processing rules and required fields (ID, SP, IdP, InResponseTo, Recipient, NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter); validate XML against hardened local schemas and select elements via absolute XPath; prevent caching of POST messages; implement replay detection and short-lived, OneTimeUse assertions; validate RelayState against an allowlist when it is a URL; validate IdP certificates (algorithm strength, expiration, revocation) and only trust configured IdPs; perform normal input validation on all SAML-related inputs; use strong, up-to-date crypto and deprecate weak XMLEnc algorithms.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure XML selection): `Element assertion = doc.getElementsByTagName("Assertion").item(0);` and trust its signature. After (safer): validate `doc` against a local hardened schema, then locate the signed assertion with an absolute XPath bound to the expected ID, and verify the signature using a preconfigured trusted IdP key, ignoring any KeyInfo from the document.
Denial-of-Service Resilience in Application and Session Design
WHAT: Applications that allow user input or sessions to drive expensive CPU, memory, storage, or thread usage (e.g., large uploads, unbounded loops, slow HTTP handling, long-lived sessions) can be forced into resource exhaustion, causing denial of service or abrupt failures.
WHY: Attackers can make the system unavailable, degrade performance, or trigger cascading failures by exhausting compute, memory, bandwidth, storage, or session resources, potentially impacting all users and dependent services.
HOW: Design for graceful degradation and fault tolerance; remove single points of failure via stateless and redundant components and bulkheads; avoid highly CPU-intensive operations on user-controlled data; handle exceptions so the system continues operating; limit session lifetimes and per-session data; cap file upload size, allowed extensions, and total request size; disallow input-driven resource allocation (threads, memory, files, loops); restrict access to expensive functionality via least privilege; and apply rate limiting and bandwidth/load limits on connections.
EXAMPLE (Java):
Before: `int[] arr = new int[userInputSize]; for (int i = 0; i < userInputSize; i++) processHeavy(data);`
After: `int size = Math.min(userInputSize, MAX_SIZE); int iterations = Math.min(size, MAX_ITER); int[] arr = new int[size]; for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) processLightweight(data);`
Ruby on Rails Command and SQL/XSS/Session/Redirect/CORS/Header/Update Security
WHAT: Risky use of eval/system-like calls, string-built SQL, raw/html_safe in views, cookie-only sessions, unvalidated redirects/render paths/CORS origins, missing security headers, and outdated dependencies can lead to command/SQL/XSS/CSRF/open-redirect and other attacks.
WHY: Exploits can allow arbitrary command/SQL execution, account/session compromise, data theft or modification, phishing via redirects, and bypass of browser protections.
HOW: Avoid eval and shelling out; if unavoidable, strictly allowlist and validate inputs. Use parameterized queries and sanitize_sql_like for SQL. Never use raw/html_safe on user input; prefer markup languages or sanitize with an allowlist plus CSP. Use :active_record_store for sensitive sessions and never store secrets in sessions. For redirects/renders, avoid user-controlled URLs/paths; if needed, use only_path or map keys to fixed URLs and validate scheme/host with anchored regexes. Configure strict CORS allowlists with rack-cors, set secure headers (X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, CSP, HSTS), and keep Rails/gems updated via a defined patching process.
EXAMPLE: Before (SQL/XSS/redirect): `@projects = Project.where("name like '" + params[:name] + "'"); redirect_to params[:url]; <%= raw @product.name %>` After: `@projects = Project.where("name like ?", "%#{ActiveRecord::Base.sanitize_sql_like(params[:name])}%"); redirect_to ACCEPTABLE_URLS[params[:url]] if ACCEPTABLE_URLS[params[:url]]; <%= @product.name %>`
Third-Party JavaScript Tag Security
WHAT: Unreviewed or dynamically changeable third-party JavaScript tags can execute arbitrary code in the user’s browser, alter the DOM, and exfiltrate sensitive data (e.g., URL parameters, cookies, page content) to external servers.
WHY: Compromised vendor/tag-manager code or misconfigured marketing tags can lead to XSS, data leakage, user tracking across sites, and full compromise of client-side behavior.
HOW: Prefer a server-controlled data layer and restrict tags to reading only from that layer; mirror third-party scripts in-house, use HTTPS, Subresource Integrity, CSP, and sandboxed iframes; disable custom HTML/JS in tag managers; validate all DOM-derived data; keep JS libraries updated; and verify vendors’ security and access controls.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `<script src="https://vendor.com/tag.js"></script>` reading `location.search` and writing directly into the page. After (more secure): host code populates a validated `dataLayer` object, tag manager is configured to read only `dataLayer` values, script is mirrored or loaded with `integrity="..."`
and `sandbox`/CSP applied to limit DOM and cookie access.
JAAS authentication and credential handling
WHAT: Mishandling of JAAS authentication state and credentials (e.g., not clearing usernames/passwords on abort, not removing principals/credentials on logout) can leave sensitive identity data resident in memory or associated with a subject after authentication fails or ends.
WHY: Residual credentials or principals can be abused to impersonate users, escalate privileges, or leak sensitive information such as usernames and passwords.
HOW: On abort(), always reset all authentication state (usernames, passwords, flags like succeeded); on logout(), always remove all principals and credentials from the Subject and ensure it is not left in a read-only state that prevents cleanup.
EXAMPLE: In abort(), explicitly null out username and overwrite password char[] before returning; in logout(), call subject.getPrincipals().clear() and subject.getPublicCredentials().clear() (and similarly for private credentials) to fully detach identity data from the Subject.
Symfony Security Practices for Web Applications
WHAT: Multiple common web vulnerabilities (XSS, CSRF, SQL/Command Injection, Open Redirect, File Upload, Path Traversal, insecure dependencies, CORS misconfig, weak headers/sessions/auth, error disclosure, secret handling) can arise if Symfony features are misused or bypassed.
WHY: Exploitation can lead to code execution, data theft or loss, account takeover, phishing, malware delivery, and compromise of servers and users.
HOW: Use Twig auto-escaping and avoid |raw on untrusted data; enable and validate CSRF tokens for all state-changing actions; use Doctrine repositories/parameterized queries instead of string-concatenated DQL/SQL; avoid exec() on user input and prefer safe filesystem APIs; validate/allowlist redirect targets; strictly validate upload type/size, store uploads outside web root with unique names; normalize and validate file paths (realpath/basename) against an allowed base directory; keep dependencies updated and run Symfony/Composer security checkers; configure CORS with explicit allowed origins/headers/methods; add and enforce security headers; harden session/cookie settings (secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, short TTL); configure providers/firewalls/access_control correctly; hide detailed errors in production; store secrets in environment variables/Symfony secrets, never in source; disable debug and enforce HTTPS in production.
EXAMPLE: In Symfony/Doctrine, do not build queries as `"SELECT p FROM App\Entity\Post p WHERE p.id = " . $id;`; instead use `$query = $em->createQuery("SELECT p FROM App\Entity\Post p WHERE p.id = :id"); $query->setParameter('id', $id);`.
Multifactor Authentication Implementation
WHAT: Failure to implement robust, independent multifactor authentication (MFA) for all authentication paths and recovery flows allows attackers who obtain or guess passwords to take over accounts, especially for admin or sensitive actions.
WHY: Compromised passwords are common; without strong MFA and secure reset/bypass procedures, attackers can perform credential stuffing, brute force, phishing-based compromise, or abuse weak recovery to bypass MFA entirely.
HOW: Require MFA for all users (and always for admin/high-privilege actions), use standards-based TOTP/U2F/FIDO2 or passkeys instead of SMS/email/security questions, enforce MFA on every login/API/mobile auth path, and design recovery with strong verification (e.g., single-use recovery codes, secondary factors, or rigorously verified support flows) so it is not weaker than normal MFA.
EXAMPLE: Before: `if (checkPassword(user, pwd)) { createSession(user); }` After: `if (checkPassword(user, pwd) && verifyMfa(user, mfaCodeOrToken)) { createSession(user); }` and ensure `/api/login` and mobile login call the same `verifyMfa` logic.
Avoid leaking secrets and sensitive files when publishing npm packages
WHAT: Secrets (API keys, passwords, .env files, tokens) and other sensitive files can be unintentionally included in published npm tarballs due to misconfigured .gitignore/.npmignore or missing allowlists.
WHY: Exposed secrets enable account takeover, data exfiltration, and compromise of production systems by anyone who installs or inspects the package.
HOW: Never store long‑lived secrets in the project tree; ensure .npmignore is updated whenever .gitignore changes; prefer an explicit files allowlist in package.json; and always run npm publish --dry-run to verify the final contents before publishing.
EXAMPLE: Before (risky): rely only on .gitignore and keep .env in the project root. After (safer): add .env to .npmignore (or move secrets outside the project), define "files": ["dist/", "lib/", "package.json", "README.md"] in package.json, and inspect the output of npm publish --dry-run.
OAuth 2.0 Security Guidelines for Implementers
WHAT: Misconfigured OAuth/OIDC clients and authorization/resource servers can expose tokens, allow code interception/replay, enable mix-up/open-redirect attacks, and over-privileged or replayable tokens.
WHY: These flaws can lead to token theft, account takeover, privilege escalation, and impersonation of resource owners or clients.
HOW: Disallow open redirectors; require PKCE (with non-plain challenge) and enforce code_verifier; use nonce/state for CSRF; avoid implicit and password grants; sender-constrain access/refresh tokens (mTLS/DPoP, rotation); enforce audience/scope/authorization_details checks per request; use asymmetric client auth; require TLS and HTTPS redirect URIs; prevent clients from influencing client_id/sub-like claims; use iss and/or distinct redirect URIs when multiple AS are used.
EXAMPLE (OAuth 2.0, HTTP): BEFORE: GET /auth?redirect_uri=https://example.com/callback?next={user_url}  // open redirect, no PKCE, response_type=token. AFTER: GET /auth?response_type=code&redirect_uri=https://example.com/callback&code_challenge={pkce_challenge}&code_challenge_method=S256&state={csrf_token}  // fixed redirect, auth code + PKCE + CSRF.
Prototype Pollution Prevention in JavaScript
WHAT: Prototype pollution occurs when attacker-controlled input can modify JavaScript object prototypes (e.g., Object.prototype), leading to unexpected properties or behavior across the application.
WHY: Polluted prototypes can cause unauthorized data access, privilege escalation, logic corruption, or remote code execution when polluted properties are later trusted or executed.
HOW: Prefer using Map/Set instead of plain objects for key/value storage; when objects are required, create them with Object.create(null) or {__proto__: null}; where safe, freeze or seal critical prototypes; in Node.js, use the --disable-proto=delete flag to remove __proto__ as a pollution vector.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): const opts = {}; opts[userInputKey] = userInputVal; // userInputKey could be "__proto__". After (safer): const opts = Object.create(null); opts[userInputKey] = userInputVal;
CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
WHAT: Failing to enforce per-object authorization when using user-controlled lookup IDs (e.g., predictable account IDs in URLs) allows attackers to access or modify other users’ resources by guessing or tampering with identifiers.
WHY: Leads to horizontal or vertical privilege escalation and Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR), exposing or corrupting sensitive data such as accounts, transactions, or PII.
HOW: Avoid exposing internal IDs when possible; use user/session-bound indirect references; and always perform server-side access control checks on every request for the specific object, not just the object type.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `/accountTransactions?acct_id=523` returns data if `acct_id` exists, without checking ownership. After (fixed): server derives the account from the authenticated user/session or, if an ID is supplied, verifies that the current user is authorized for that specific account before returning any data.
XSS filter evasion and incomplete input filtering
WHAT: Relying on input filtering or regex-based blacklists to block specific XSS patterns (e.g., `javascript:`, `<script>`, certain encodings) is an incomplete defense; attackers can bypass such filters using alternate encodings, malformed tags, event handlers, protocol tricks, and HTTP parameter pollution.
WHY: Bypassed filters allow execution of arbitrary script in the victim’s browser (stored, reflected, or DOM-based XSS), leading to session theft, account takeover, CSRF, data exfiltration, and arbitrary actions as the user.
HOW: Do not depend on XSS filters or WAF signatures as primary protection; instead, contextually encode all untrusted data on output (HTML, attribute, JS, URL contexts), use safe templating, apply strict input validation/allowlists for URLs and parameters, avoid reflecting raw query parameters into HTML/JS, and validate/encode all redirect targets and query parameters (including those affected by HTTP Parameter Pollution).
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe, reflected into JS): `var title = "<%= $_GET['title'] %>";` → After (safe): `var title = "<%= Encode.forJavaScript(Encode.forHtml($_GET['title'])) %>";`
GraphQL API Security Guidelines
WHAT: GraphQL APIs are vulnerable to injection, DoS, broken access control/IDOR, batching/brute-force attacks, and information leakage via insecure defaults (introspection, GraphiQL, verbose errors).
WHY: Exploitation can lead to data theft or modification, remote code/command execution, account takeover, large-scale enumeration, and loss of availability through resource exhaustion.
HOW: Strictly validate and allowlist all inputs with appropriate GraphQL types/custom validators; use safe APIs (parameterized queries/ORMs) or proper escaping for downstream interpreters; never use user input to control hosts/critical data flow; enforce depth/amount limits, pagination, timeouts, query-cost and rate limiting; constrain CPU/memory; implement robust authorization on every resolver, edge, and node (including ID-based access); disable or tightly restrict introspection, GraphiQL, typo-suggestion, debug/stack traces in production; and add code-level limits or disable batching for sensitive objects.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe SQL): `db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + args.id);` After (safe): `db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", [args.id]);` plus a schema constraint: `type Query { user(id: ID!): User }` with a resolver that checks `currentUser.canViewUser(args.id)` before querying.
Injection Prevention in Application Code
WHAT: Injection flaws occur when untrusted input is sent to interpreters (SQL, LDAP, OS shell, etc.) as part of commands or queries, allowing attackers to alter queries, execute commands, or bypass controls.
WHY: Successful injection can expose or modify sensitive data, execute arbitrary OS commands, escalate privileges, or compromise entire systems.
HOW: For any user-controlled data used in queries/commands: (1) Prefer safe APIs with parameterized interfaces (e.g., prepared statements, safely written stored procedures, ProcessBuilder with separate args); (2) Apply strict allowlist validation for commands, arguments, table/column names, and other dynamic elements; (3) If parameterization is impossible, contextually escape all untrusted data using the correct escaping rules for that interpreter (SQL, LDAP DN/search, shell, etc.); (4) Avoid building dynamic query/command strings via concatenation, especially inside stored procedures or eval-like constructs.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe, SQL): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + userInput + "'";` After (safe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"; pstmt = conn.prepareStatement(query); pstmt.setString(1, userInput);`
RESTful Web Service Attack Surface Identification and Fuzzing
WHAT: Failure to correctly identify and fuzz all RESTful endpoints and non-standard parameters (URL segments, headers, JSON/XML fields) can leave exploitable inputs untested and vulnerable.
WHY: Unfuzzed or misclassified parameters may contain injection, authorization, or logic flaws that attackers can exploit to access or manipulate data or functions.
HOW: Enumerate endpoints and parameters using any available documentation/configuration, then capture full requests via a proxy (including headers and bodies); classify URL segments, headers, and structured bodies as parameters by looking for repeating/varying patterns and verifying with invalid values; prioritize fuzzing on identified parameters, focusing on boundary and out-of-range values while correctly emulating the authentication mechanism.
EXAMPLE: (Pattern) For URLs like `http://server/src/XXXX/page` where `XXXX` varies widely, treat `XXXX` as a parameter and fuzz it with edge-case values while maintaining valid auth tokens in headers.
Secure coding and configuration for applications
WHAT: Applications may be vulnerable if code lacks input validation, secure error handling, proper authz/authn, safe cryptography, least-privilege execution, secure memory management, secret management, testing, and reviews, or if runtime configuration is insecure (over-privileged, insecure defaults, weak comms, poor data protection).
WHY: These failures can lead to injection, memory corruption, data breaches, privilege escalation, service compromise, and increased blast radius when components or connections are attacked.
HOW: Validate and sanitize all inputs; handle errors without leaking sensitive data; enforce strong authentication and fine-grained authorization; use approved cryptographic libraries and protocols; run code and services with least privilege; avoid hardcoded secrets by using secure secret stores; perform security testing, code review, and keep dependencies updated; configure systems to be secure-by-default, fail securely, use encrypted channels, and restrict access and permissions.
EXAMPLE (Java):
Before: `String query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + request.getParameter("id"); stmt.executeQuery(query);`
After: `String query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=?"; PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(query); ps.setInt(1, Integer.parseInt(request.getParameter("id"))); ps.executeQuery();`
Zero Trust access control for applications and APIs
WHAT: Failing to enforce strong, per-request authentication and authorization for applications and APIs, including legacy systems, allows attackers with network access or stolen credentials to call internal services, move laterally, or exfiltrate data.
WHY: Missing or weak identity checks, schema validation, and segmentation enable credential abuse, API-first attacks, and exploitation of legacy apps, leading to data theft and system compromise.
HOW: Require MFA-backed identity for every session and every API call; use identity-aware proxies, WAFs, and API gateways to authenticate each request, validate request schemas, enforce least-privilege and just-in-time access, and micro-segment apps so only explicitly allowed, encrypted traffic is permitted; front legacy systems with security proxies that add modern auth and logging.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): an internal API endpoint accepts requests from any host on the internal network with only a static API key and no schema validation; After (secure): the same endpoint is placed behind an API gateway that requires OAuth2 access tokens tied to user/device identity, validates JSON schemas, enforces per-client rate limits, and logs all access.
Secure security-event logging vocabulary
WHAT: Failure to use a consistent, security-focused logging vocabulary for key events (authn/z, sessions, uploads, sensitive data, system/user changes, malicious behavior) makes it hard to detect, correlate, and investigate attacks.
WHY: Inconsistent or missing security logs delay breach detection and response, hinder forensics, and can hide account takeover, privilege escalation, data exfiltration, and abuse of business logic.
HOW: Define and enforce a standard event schema (fields like datetime in ISO 8601 with UTC offset, appid, event, level, description, useragent, IPs, URI, method, region) and a fixed set of event names/prefixes (e.g., authn_login_fail, authz_fail, upload_validation, sensitive_read, session_use_after_expire, malicious_*); instrument all relevant code paths to emit these events with appropriate severity, and avoid logging secrets or highly sensitive data unless strictly necessary and compliant with privacy rules.
EXAMPLE: Before: ad‑hoc logs like `log("login error", user)` or no logs on authz failure. After: `log_event("authn_login_fail:joebob1", level="WARN", description="User joebob1 login failed", request_uri="/api/v2/auth/", source_ip=ip, useragent=ua, datetime=now_iso8601_utc_offset)` and `log_event("authz_fail:joebob1,/admin", level="CRITICAL", description="Unauthorized admin access attempt")`.
Secure CI/CD Pipelines and Secrets
WHAT: CI/CD pipelines, SCM, and execution environments may be misconfigured, over-privileged, or leak secrets (e.g., hardcoded credentials, logging secrets, unreviewed config/merge) leading to unauthorized code execution or deployment.
WHY: Compromise of CI/CD or its secrets can give attackers high-privilege access to source code, infrastructure, and production systems, enabling supply-chain attacks and data breaches.
HOW: Harden CI/CD and SCM (no default configs; protected branches; mandatory reviews; MFA; least-privilege identities; isolated build nodes; TLS 1.2+; IP restrictions), manage secrets via dedicated vaults (no hardcoding, always encrypted, never logged/printed), pin and verify dependency versions and hashes, tightly govern plugins/integrations, and enable centralized, sanitized logging and monitoring.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `password = "ProdDBPass123"` in repo; pipeline prints `$password` in logs and runs as root with `docker --privileged`. After (secure): password stored in Vault and injected as an environment variable only at runtime, pipeline masks the variable in logs, runs in an isolated non-root container without `--privileged`, and uses a minimally scoped service account.
Attack Surface Management for Applications
WHAT: Failing to identify, measure, and control all entry/exit points, exposed components, and sensitive data paths leads to an unnecessarily large and poorly understood attack surface.
WHY: An expanded or undocumented attack surface increases the likelihood and impact of remote exploitation, data exfiltration, privilege abuse, and compromise of backups or legacy components.
HOW: Continuously map and bucket all external- and internal-facing endpoints, user roles, and sensitive data; prioritize internet-facing and high-privilege paths; remove or disable unused features, versions, and backups; enforce strong authz/authn, validation, logging, and encryption on all exposed paths; trigger threat modeling and focused testing whenever new endpoint types, roles, or architectural changes are introduced.
EXAMPLE: Before: leaving deprecated admin APIs, old backup endpoints, and unused upload features reachable from the internet. After: removing or firewalling deprecated endpoints, disabling unused uploads, restricting admin APIs to authenticated admins on internal networks, and updating the attack-surface map and tests to cover only the intended exposed interfaces.
CSS information disclosure via global, descriptive selectors
WHAT: Global CSS files with role-specific, descriptive selectors (e.g., .addUser, .deleteAdmin) are publicly accessible and leak internal features, roles, and permissions to unauthenticated users.
WHY: Attackers can use leaked selector names and structure for reconnaissance, mapping features and privileged actions to plan targeted attacks or privilege escalation.
HOW: Split CSS by access-control level (e.g., Student.css, Admin.css), enforce authorization checks before serving each CSS file, log/alert on forced browsing attempts, and avoid descriptive/role-revealing selector names by using generic, obfuscated, or library-provided classes.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): public/styles/global.css with .addUser, .deleteAdmin, .exportUserData used across all pages; After (more secure): serve /styles/admin.min.css with obfuscated classes (e.g., .c001, .c002) only to authenticated admins via server-side access control.
Prompt Injection Prevention in LLM-Integrated Applications
WHAT: LLM prompts are constructed by directly concatenating system instructions with user-controlled input, allowing attackers to inject instructions that override system prompts, exfiltrate data, or trigger unauthorized tool/API actions.
WHY: Successful prompt injection can bypass safety controls, leak system prompts and secrets (e.g., API keys), perform unauthorized operations via tools, and persist across sessions, leading to data breaches and compromised systems.
HOW: Separate instructions from data using structured prompts; validate and sanitize all user/external inputs (including encoded/obfuscated text) with pattern and fuzzy matching; monitor and filter outputs for leakage patterns; enforce least-privilege on tools/APIs; add human-in-the-loop review for high-risk requests; log and rate-limit interactions and regularly test with known attack patterns.
EXAMPLE:
Before (vulnerable, unstructured):
full_prompt = system_prompt + "\n\nUser: " + user_input
After (safer, structured + filtering):
clean = input_filter.sanitize_input(user_input)
prompt = create_structured_prompt(system_prompt, clean)
resp = llm.generate(prompt)
return output_validator.filter_response(resp)
Django REST API hardening
WHAT: In Django REST Framework, insecure defaults and unsafe patterns (e.g., AllowAny permissions, no throttling, broad serializers/forms, unsafe YAML/SQL/exec usage, hardcoded secrets, weak logging) can lead to unauthorized access, data exposure, DoS, injection, and compromised environments.
WHY: These issues allow attackers to read/modify other users’ data, brute-force or hijack accounts, exhaust resources, execute arbitrary code/queries, abuse undocumented APIs, and evade detection.

EXAMPLE:
Before (unsafe permissions & auth):
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
"DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES": [],
"DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES": ["rest_framework.permissions.AllowAny"],
"DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES": [],
}
After (hardened):
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
"DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES": [
"rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication",
"rest_framework.authentication.TokenAuthentication",
],
"DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES": [
"rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated",
],
"DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES": [
"rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle",
"rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle",
],
}
Strong cryptography for user data and credentials
WHAT: Failure to encrypt user communications and private data in transit and at rest, or storing passwords without strong, work-factor-adjusted, collision-resistant hashing.
WHY: Exposed or intercepted data/credentials enable account takeover, privacy violations, and long-term compromise even if databases or channels are later secured.
HOW: Enforce TLS/SSL with verified certificates, strong ciphers, and sufficient key lengths for all authenticated and sensitive endpoints; encrypt sensitive data at rest with strong keys under strict access control; always hash passwords with modern adaptive algorithms (e.g., bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) and tune work factors regularly.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): store plaintext password or send credentials over HTTP; After (secure): use HTTPS-only endpoints and store only password_hash = bcrypt(password, work_factor).
HTML5 secure communication and storage
WHAT: In HTML5 features (postMessage, CORS, WebSockets, SSE, storage, workers, iframes, JWT-based WS APIs), unvalidated origins, unsafe DOM insertion/eval, weak CORS rules, insecure ws://, storing sensitive data client-side, and unauthenticated/unchecked messages can lead to XSS, CSRF-like abuse, hijacking, data theft, and token misuse.
WHY: Exploitation can allow cross-site scripting, cross-origin data exfiltration, account/session compromise, CSWSH, man-in-the-middle attacks, privilege escalation, and long-lived stolen tokens.
HOW: Always validate exact expected origins and URLs; treat all cross-origin and client-stored data as untrusted; never eval or innerHTML untrusted data (use textContent/JSON.parse); restrict CORS (no * for sensitive data, strict allowlist, CSRF defenses); use only RFC 6455 over wss:// and check Origin plus full input validation/JSON Schema; require explicit, signed tokens (e.g., JWT) on each WS message, validate claims and blocklisted tokens, and close insecure sessions; avoid storing sensitive data/session IDs in localStorage/IndexedDB; sandbox untrusted iframes and use X-Frame-Options; disable autocomplete/caching for credential/PII fields.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe postMessage receive): `window.addEventListener('message', e => eval(e.data));` After (safe): `window.addEventListener('message', e => { if (e.origin !== 'https://example.com') return; if (!isValidMessage(e.data)) return; handleMessage(e.data); });`
Cloud object storage access control
WHAT: In code that accesses cloud object storage, overly broad IAM policies, hardcoded credentials, or custom signed-URL generation that accepts injectable input can expose sensitive data or allow anonymous access to protected objects.
WHY: Compromised or misused credentials and weak URL-signing logic can let attackers read/modify private data, abuse control-plane APIs, or perform code-injection attacks via crafted URLs.
HOW: Use least-privilege IAM roles for storage access, never hardcode credentials (use instance/role-based identities), rely on provider SDKs for signed URLs, strictly validate/encode any data used in URL signing, and set short expirations for signed URLs containing non-public data.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): application embeds long-lived access keys and builds signed URLs by concatenating user-controlled path strings; After (secure): application uses a role-based identity from the runtime environment, constructs object keys from validated/allowlisted inputs, and calls the cloud SDK’s signing API with a minimal-scope policy and a short TTL.
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Defense
WHAT: User-controlled URLs, IPs, or domains are used by the server to make outbound requests, allowing attackers to reach internal services, metadata endpoints, or non-HTTP protocols if inputs, redirects, and DNS/IP handling are not strictly controlled.
WHY: Successful SSRF can expose internal networks, access tokens, cloud metadata, and internal APIs, enabling data exfiltration, lateral movement, and full environment compromise.
HOW: Prefer allowlists of exact IPs/domains/protocols where feasible; otherwise use strict blocklists of private/local ranges. Validate inputs with battle-tested libraries (no custom complex regex), compare against allowlists/blocklists after normalization, and disable HTTP redirects in HTTP clients. Do not accept full URLs when possible; accept only validated IP/domain plus protocol from an allowlist. Avoid DNS resolution during validation where possible; when required, resolve via controlled resolvers, verify all A/AAAA records are public, and monitor allowlisted domains for resolution to internal/non-global IPs. Enforce that internal domains resolve only via internal DNS and that internal DNS does not resolve external domains. In cloud, enable IMDSv2 (AWS) and disable IMDSv1. Use static analysis (e.g., Semgrep SSRF rules) to detect unsafe request patterns.
EXAMPLE (Java):
Before: `URL url = new URL(userUrl); HttpURLConnection c = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection(); c.setInstanceFollowRedirects(true);`
After: `URI u = new URI(userHost); if (!ALLOWED_HOSTS.contains(u.getHost())) reject(); HttpURLConnection c = (HttpURLConnection) new URL("https", u.getHost(), path).openConnection(); c.setInstanceFollowRedirects(false);`
JWT security guidelines
WHAT: JWTs can be forged, replayed, leaked, or misused if algorithms, secrets, storage, revocation, and token contents are handled insecurely (e.g., accepting alg=none, weak HMAC secrets, readable sensitive claims, stolen tokens, or non‑revocable tokens).
WHY: Exploitation can lead to account takeover, privilege escalation (e.g., role=admin), token replay, information disclosure about internal systems, and inability to log out stolen sessions.
HOW: Use a modern, patched JWT library; explicitly pin the expected signing algorithm on verification; use strong (≥64‑char, random) HMAC secrets or asymmetric keys; encrypt tokens (e.g., AES‑GCM via a vetted library) if claims are sensitive; bind tokens to a user context (random fingerprint in hardened HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookie, hash stored in claim and checked on each request); implement server‑side revocation (denylist of token digests) or sidejacking‑resistant logout; and store tokens in sessionStorage or JS closures and send them only as Authorization: Bearer headers, with CSP and short expirations/rotation if using localStorage.
EXAMPLE: In Java, verify with a pinned algorithm and context: `JWTVerifier v = JWT.require(Algorithm.HMAC256(keyHMAC)).withIssuer(issuerID).withClaim("userFingerprint", userFingerprintHash).build(); DecodedJWT jwt = v.verify(token);`
Certificate/Public-Key Pinning in Applications
WHAT: Misconfigured or ad‑hoc certificate/public-key pinning can cause MITM vulnerabilities (if pins are bypassable or tainted) or application outages (if pins cannot be updated safely).
WHY: Incorrect pinning lets attackers with rogue or injected CAs intercept/modify traffic, or can brick clients when certificates/keys rotate and the pinset cannot be updated.
HOW: Only pin when you fully control both client and server and can update pinsets securely; prefer preloading pins at development time; pin leaf certificates or subjectPublicKeyInfo with backup pins; never allow users to bypass pin failures; use platform pinning APIs/libraries (e.g., Android Network Security Config, TrustKit, electron-ssl-pinning) instead of custom validation; on TLS connect callbacks, verify the peer certificate/key matches one of the configured pins and hard-fail the connection otherwise.
EXAMPLE: (Android) Use Network Security Configuration with a <pin-set> in XML instead of custom X509TrustManager logic, and ensure that when the certificate changes you ship an updated configuration before or in lockstep with server rotation.
Browser Extension Security Guidelines
WHAT: Browser extensions may over-request permissions, leak or expose sensitive data (including via DOM or prototype-based skimming), use insecure communication/storage, inject or load untrusted code, lack strict CSP, rely on vulnerable dependencies, or mishandle privacy controls, leading to data theft or account compromise.
WHY: These issues let attackers read or exfiltrate browsing activity and personal data, execute arbitrary code, hijack extension behavior, or violate privacy regulations, especially if a page or dependency is compromised.
HOW: Request only minimal required and optional permissions; avoid rendering or handling sensitive data in page context/DOM; use HTTPS and encrypt stored secrets; avoid eval/remote scripts and restrict script sources with a strict CSP; keep dependencies updated and audited; sign and verify updates; and provide clear, opt‑in privacy controls and data minimization.
EXAMPLE: Before (overreach + insecure): `"permissions": ["tabs","http://*/*","https://*/*","storage"]`, `fetch('http://example.com/track', { body: JSON.stringify({ URL: tab.url }) });` and `localStorage.setItem('token', token);`. After (least privilege + secure): `"permissions": ["storage"]`, request host permissions only when needed via `optional_permissions`, send only non-sensitive data over `https://...` with user consent, and store encrypted tokens via the browser’s extension storage API.
HTTP Security Response Headers Configuration
WHAT: Missing, misconfigured, or deprecated HTTP security headers (e.g., CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, CORS, COOP/COEP/CORP, Permissions-Policy) can enable XSS, clickjacking, data exfiltration, Spectre-style attacks, and information disclosure.
WHY: Incorrect headers can allow content injection, unauthorized framing, cross-origin data leaks, downgrade/MITM attacks, or leak server technology details that aid attackers.
HOW: For all HTML pages, set: `Content-Security-Policy` (with `frame-ancestors` and no inline JS), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload`, `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`, `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`, `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-site`, `Permissions-Policy` disabling unused features, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with explicit origins (no `*` unless truly public), and remove/neutralize `Server`, `X-Powered-By`, `X-AspNet-Version`, `X-AspNetMvc-Version`; do not use deprecated/unsafe headers like HPKP or Expect-CT, and disable X-XSS-Protection (`X-XSS-Protection: 0`).
EXAMPLE: In a web server config, add headers such as:
`Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'`
`Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload`
SQL injection prevention for database access
WHAT: Dynamic SQL queries built via string concatenation with user-controlled input (e.g., request parameters appended directly into SQL/HQL) allow attackers to inject and execute arbitrary SQL commands.
WHY: Successful SQL injection can expose, modify, or destroy sensitive data, escalate privileges, or take full control of the database and underlying system accounts.
HOW: Use parameterized queries or safely implemented stored procedures for all user-supplied values; never concatenate raw input into SQL. For dynamic identifiers (table/column/sort order), map user input to a fixed allow-list or redesign to avoid user-controlled identifiers. Enforce least-privilege DB accounts (separate users per app/feature, no DBA/admin rights, prefer views for restricted access). Avoid relying solely on escaping; use input validation as a secondary defense only.

// String q = "SELECT account_balance FROM user_data WHERE user_name = '" + request.getParameter("customerName") + "'";
// Safe (Java)
// String q = "SELECT account_balance FROM user_data WHERE user_name = ?"; PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(q); ps.setString(1, request.getParameter("customerName"));
HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) configuration
WHAT: Failing to configure HSTS (or misconfiguring max-age/includeSubDomains/preload) allows HTTP access, invalid-certificate click-through, and cookie-related attacks via downgraded or intercepted connections.
WHY: Attackers can perform man-in-the-middle attacks, strip TLS (sslstrip), or manipulate cookies from non-HSTS subdomains, leading to credential theft, session hijacking, and privacy leaks.
HOW: Always serve the HSTS header over HTTPS with a sufficiently long max-age, and enable includeSubDomains once all subdomains support HTTPS; optionally use preload only after confirming you will not need HTTP again and understand its permanence; set the Secure flag on all cookies.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000`

WHY: Successful attacks lead to account compromise, fraud, data theft, and abuse of privileged or financial operations, often at large scale and from distributed botnets.
HOW: Implement MFA (with risk-based step-up), layered defenses (CAPTCHA, IP and connection/device fingerprinting, leaked-password checks, unpredictable usernames, multi-step login, JavaScript challenges, and controlled degradation), and central monitoring/metrics; tune thresholds by role and risk, avoid user enumeration, and coordinate operations across teams.

Before: `stored = hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()`

WHY: Enables phishing (trusted-domain links sending users to malicious sites) and bypass of access control by forwarding attackers to administrative or otherwise unauthorized functions.

Map short IDs/tokens to server-side URL allowlists, or strictly validate user-supplied targets against a whitelist of trusted hosts/paths or regexes, and ensure the target is authorized for the current user. Optionally interpose a warning/confirmation page before leaving the site.

WHAT: Transaction authorization can be bypassed or manipulated if critical checks, data, and flows are controlled or modifiable by the client, reused across operations, or not tightly bound to the specific transaction and step sequence.
WHY: Attackers can authorize fraudulent transactions, downgrade authorization methods, brute-force or replay credentials, alter transaction data (TOCTOU), or execute transactions without proper user consent, leading to financial loss and account compromise.

EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): client sends {amount, target, otp}; server checks only otp and user session, allowing client to change amount/target after OTP generation or reuse OTP for multiple transfers. After (secure): server stores {amount, target, nonce} when user initiates; generates a one-time challenge bound to that stored data and step; client returns response; server verifies response, confirms stored data unchanged, checks step order and nonce unused and unexpired, then executes exactly the stored transaction.

WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
CMD "npm" "start"
After (safer):

RUN apk add dumb-init

Threat modeling in the SDLC
WHAT: Failing to perform structured threat modeling leads to unrecognized spoofing, tampering, information disclosure, repudiation, denial of service, and privilege escalation risks in the system design.
WHY: Undiscovered design-level threats become expensive or impossible to fix later, enabling attackers to exploit trust boundaries, data flows, and weak mitigations across the application.

WHAT: Pages are vulnerable to clickjacking if they can be loaded in a frame/iframe by untrusted sites, allowing attackers to trick users into clicking hidden UI elements.

WHAT: Misconfigured or disabled Django security features (auth, CSRF, XSS, HTTPS, cookies, headers, key management) can expose the app to common web attacks such as brute force, credential theft, session hijacking, CSRF, XSS, clickjacking, and insecure transport.

Before (insecure): DEBUG = True; SECRET_KEY = 'hardcoded'; SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False; MIDDLEWARE = []; SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = False
After (hardened): DEBUG = False; SECRET_KEY = os.environ['DJANGO_SECRET_KEY']; SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True; CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True; MIDDLEWARE += ['django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware','django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware','django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware']; SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True; X_FRAME_OPTIONS = 'DENY'

Before: `http://api.example.com/login?apiKey=abc123` and accept JWT with header `{"alg":"none"}`.
After: `https://api.example.com/login` with `Authorization: Bearer <signed-JWT>` in header, server pins acceptable algorithms in config, validates iss/aud/exp/nbf, and rejects any token whose hash is on a logout denylist.

WHAT: In microservice-based systems, missing or incomplete documentation of services, data assets, and their interactions leads to insecure design decisions, excessive privileges, untested attack surface, and unprotected sensitive data flows.
WHY: Poor architectural visibility prevents effective threat modeling, least-privilege enforcement, data leakage prevention, and centralized security control verification, increasing risk of data exposure and lateral movement.
HOW: For each microservice, infrastructure service, storage, message queue, and data asset, maintain version-controlled records of IDs, purpose, APIs (with auth scopes/keys), data classifications, and all service-to-service, service-to-storage, and asset-to-storage relations; use these to drive threat modeling, attack-surface enumeration, and permission design.

After: A registry defines each service’s API (with required scopes), its read/write storages, its sync/async peers, and the protection level of each asset, and developers restrict new calls and credentials to the minimal documented needs.

WHAT: Constructing OS command strings from user-controlled input (including arguments) without proper separation, parameterization, or validation allows attackers to inject additional commands or options that the program did not intend to run.
WHY: Successful command or argument injection can lead to information disclosure, arbitrary command execution, and potentially full remote code execution, especially if the process runs with elevated privileges.

WHAT: Insecure cryptographic storage (e.g., reversible password encryption, weak/incorrect algorithms or modes, predictable randomness, hard‑coded or co‑located keys) exposes sensitive data and keys to theft or misuse.
WHY: Attackers who obtain weakly protected data or keys can recover passwords, decrypt data at rest, forge tokens, or escalate access even if other controls fail.

WHY: Leads to privilege escalation or unauthorized access (e.g., anonymous or basic users successfully calling admin-only endpoints like DeleteMessage).
HOW: Maintain a technology-independent authorization matrix (e.g., XML pivot file listing roles, services, allowed HTTP methods and expected allow/deny status codes) and implement automated integration tests that, for each logical role, call every service and assert the response code matches the matrix; run these tests on every release.

WHAT: Insecure cryptographic key management (e.g., plaintext key storage, uncontrolled access, weak lifecycle controls, or misuse of keys for multiple purposes) can expose keys to theft, misuse, or loss, breaking confidentiality, integrity, and availability of protected data.
WHY: Compromised or lost keys can permanently expose all encrypted data, enable forgery of signatures and certificates, prevent data recovery, and undermine trust in the system and its identities.
